title: Lesson 6
subtitle: Wanting and Not Wanting — Conjugating adjectives
objectives: Say you want something with [thing] ga hoshii desu
Say you don't want something by dropping い and adding ku nai: hoshiku nai desu
Conjugate i-adjectives (and color adjectives) into the negative form with ku nai
Keep ja nai for nouns and ku nai for i-adjectives — never mix them up
Use no to string modifiers together: watashi no tomodachi no Akiko san
Count money: hyaku en, sen doru
Read hiragana は ひ ふ へ ほ with dakuten and handakuten, and spot the special topic-marker reading wa

vocab.english: Please come in / (Hai) douzo: Here you are (when serving or giving something)
I will come in (literally, 'I will bother you,' when entering someone's house)

vocab.japanese: ちょっとまってください

grammar.title: Making i-adjectives negative
grammar.pattern: (i-adjective) minus い, add くない
grammar.explanation: Ja nai (from the prior lesson) is used with nouns, but it cannot be used with i-adjectives. All true adjectives end with an い. To make an i-adjective negative, drop the last い then add ku nai.

examples.japanese: あたらしい → あたらしくない
おいしい → おいしくない
あつい → あつくない
つめたい → つめたくない
examples.english: cold to the touch → not cold to the touch

mistakes: Using ja nai with i-adjectives — ja nai is used with nouns and ku nai with i-adjectives
Forgetting to drop the final い before adding ku nai

grammar.title: The colors as negative adjectives
grammar.pattern: [color] minus い, add くない
grammar.explanation: The same rule applies to the adjective forms of colors: drop the final い and add ku nai.

examples.japanese: あかい → あかくない
あおい → あおくない
ちゃいろい → ちゃいろくない
きいろい → きいろくない

mistakes: Treating colors like nouns and adding ja nai instead of ku nai

grammar.title: Wanting and not wanting
grammar.pattern: [thing] ga hoshii desu / [thing] ga hoshiku nai desu
grammar.explanation: The particle ga is used with hoshii (want) in the same way it is used with suki and kirai. Ga marks the thing that you want or don't want. To change 'want' into 'don't want,' drop the い then add ku nai.

examples.japanese: あたらしいテレビがほしいです。
つめたいのみものがほしいです。
ふるいくるまがほしくないです。
examples.romaji: Furui kuruma ga hoshiku nai desu.
examples.english: I don't want an old car.

mistakes: Using a particle other than ga to mark the thing you want

grammar.title: Tricky uses of the particle no
grammar.explanation: No shows possession, and it can also turn any noun into an adjective (modifier) for the word after it. In a string of no's, keep in mind the key function: no makes the word before it modify what comes after. Watashi no tomodachi no Akiko san simply means 'my friend Akiko' — watashi no tomodachi just modifies Akiko san.

examples.japanese: わたしのともだちのあきこさんは にじゅうさいです。
examples.romaji: Watashi no tomodachi no Akiko san wa nijuusai desu.
examples.english: My friend Akiko is 25 years old.

mistakes: Reading every no as possession when it may just be marking a modifier

grammar.title: Numbers and money
grammar.explanation: To say amounts like 100 yen or 100 dollars, just add en or doru after the number. The particle no is not required.

examples.japanese: ひゃくえん
せんドル
いちまんドル

mistakes: Adding a particle between the number and en/doru

grammar.title: Culture Clip: kun and chan
grammar.explanation: Kun or chan added to the end of last or first names show affection, but are not limited to just that. Chan is mostly used after girls' names and kun after boys' names. Chan is used quite often after children's names regardless of sex, and it is not unusual for a higher-up in a company to refer to female staff members with kun after their names. Chan and kun should never be used when addressing people above you in social status — if you hear someone using them, you can assume the speaker is equal or higher in status.

examples.japanese: くん
examples.english: affectionate suffix, mostly after boys' names

examples.japanese: ちゃん
examples.english: affectionate suffix, mostly after girls' and children's names

mistakes: Using kun or chan when addressing someone above you in social status

grammar.title: Hiragana は ひ ふ へ ほ (+ dakuten and handakuten)
grammar.pattern: ha hi fu he ho; + dakuten → ba bi bu be bo; + handakuten (maru) → pa pi pu pe po
grammar.explanation: The ha row of hiragana. The pa pi pu pe po characters are made by adding a small circle where dakuten normally goes; the circle is written clockwise and is always the last stroke. Most Japanese people call it maru ('circle'); its official name is handakuten. This book represents ふ as FU instead of HU because the pronunciation is closer to FU (voiced softer than the English F). There is an easy way to write ふ: connect the first and second stroke into what looks like a number '3.'

examples.japanese: は → ば
ひ → ぴ

mistakes: Writing ふ as HU in romaji for this course
Adding the handakuten circle before the base strokes — it is always the last stroke

grammar.title: Special usage: topic marker は (wa)
grammar.explanation: The topic marker 'wa' is written using the は (ha) character and can never be written using わ (wa). In all other situations, は is always read as 'ha.' Similarly, the direction marker 'e' is written with へ (he), never え (e) — that grammar point is covered in Lesson 12.

examples.japanese: あなたはだれですか。
バナナはきいろです。
がっこうへいきます。

mistakes: Writing the topic marker as わ instead of は

exercises.prompt: Match the new words with their meanings:

exercises.explanation: Ga is used with hoshii in the same way it is used with suki and kirai.

exercises.prompt: I want money: ___ ga hoshii desu.
exercises.explanation: Okane ga hoshii desu = I want money; ga marks the thing wanted.

exercises.prompt: みずがほしいです
exercises.explanation: Mizu ga hoshii desu = I want water.

exercises.prompt: How do you make an i-adjective negative?
choices: Add ja nai to the whole word
Drop the last い then add ku nai
Add arimasen without changing the word
exercises.explanation: All true adjectives end with い: drop the last い then add ku nai.

exercises.prompt: It is not hot: atsui minus い plus ___ (roomaji).
exercises.explanation: Atsui → atsuku nai = not hot.

choices: I don't want an old car.
I don't want a new car.

exercises.prompt: After whose names is chan MOSTLY used?
exercises.explanation: Chan is mostly used after girls' names and kun after boys' names; chan is also used often after children's names regardless of sex.

exercises.prompt: With whom should you NEVER use kun or chan?
choices: people above you in social status
exercises.explanation: Chan and kun should never be used when addressing people above you in social status.

exercises.explanation: Kekkou desu = I'm fine (No thanks) — the lesson's new phrase.

exercises.prompt: How do you say '100 yen'?
exercises.explanation: Just add en after the number: hyaku en. The particle no is not required.

exercises.prompt: 1000 dollars: ___ doru. (roomaji)
exercises.explanation: Sen doru = 1000 dollars; add doru after the number.

exercises.prompt: なにがほしいですか

exercises.explanation: Dore ga hoshii desu ka = Which one do you want? (from the Q&A section)

exercises.prompt: Is your car new? No, it's not new: Iie, atarashiku ___ desu.
exercises.explanation: Iie, atarashiku nai desu = No, it's not new — atarashii minus い plus ku nai.

exercises.prompt: 'Watashi no tomodachi no Akiko san wa nijuusai desu' means...
choices: My friend Akiko is 25 years old.
My friend Akiko likes the color blue.
exercises.explanation: The no's build a modifier chain: watashi no tomodachi modifies Akiko san — 'my friend Akiko.'

exercises.prompt: Why isn't ふ written as HU in this book?
choices: The pronunciation of ふ is closer to FU (voiced softer than English F)
HU is only used for long vowels
exercises.explanation: Japanese people sometimes write HU in romaji, but the pronunciation is closer to FU.

exercises.prompt: Which character MUST be used to write the topic marker 'wa'?
exercises.explanation: The topic marker wa is written with は (ha) and can never be written with わ (wa).

exercises.explanation: Anata wa dare desu ka = Who are you? — は here is the topic marker wa.

exercises.explanation: Connect the first and second strokes into a '3' shape.

exercises.explanation: Nani ga hoshii desu ka = What do you want?

I like apples that are not red.

exercises.explanation: Akaku nai = not red (akai minus い plus ku nai); suki ja nai desu = don't like.

quiz.prompt: Ku nai is used with ___, and ja nai with ___.
quiz.explanation: The teacher's note: ja nai is used with nouns and ku nai is used with i-adjectives.
Okane ga hoshii desu = I want money.

quiz.prompt: I don't want water: Mizu ga hoshi ___ desu. (roomaji)
quiz.explanation: Drop the い of hoshii and add ku nai: hoshiku nai desu = don't want.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I want a new television'?
choices: Atarashii terebi wa hoshii desu ka.
quiz.explanation: [thing] ga hoshii desu with the i-adjective before the noun: Atarashii terebi ga hoshii desu.

quiz.explanation: Dakuten turns ha hi fu he ho into ba bi bu be bo.
Koora ga hoshii desu = I want a cola.

summary: Ga marks the thing you want: [thing] ga hoshii desu. To not want, drop the い of hoshii and add ku nai. The same rule negatives every i-adjective (atsui → atsuku nai) and the colors (akai → akaku nai) — ja nai stays with nouns. Numbers + en/doru need no particle (hyaku en, sen doru). New hiragana: は ひ ふ へ ほ, with dakuten (ば row) and handakuten/maru (ぱ row); the topic marker wa is written は, never わ.
